section_summary: This section covers proposals for Japanese tax and budget reform, cotton financing, securities regulation, and reparations. Its largest document is a Bank of Japan report estimating the production, trade, and foreign credit needed for Japan to reach a minimum self-supporting economy by mid-1950. The report continues beyond page 400.

subfiles.title: Recommendations on Japanese taxation and government finance
subfiles.about: Recommends less inflationary finance, progressive taxes, and separate taxation to fund reparations compensation.
subfiles.summary: The surviving conclusion urges bond financing instead of Bank of Japan overdrafts, reform of income and consumption taxes, stronger collection, and wider local taxing powers. It argues that reparations compensation should be funded by a special tax rather than current revenue.

subfiles.title: Shanghai telegram on proposed American loans to Japan
subfiles.about: Relays a press report on possible large American loans and credits for Japan.
subfiles.summary: The telegram quotes Wall Street Journal correspondent Ray Cromley on proposed long-term loans to close Japan’s import-export gap and short-term credit for raw materials, especially cotton.

subfiles.title: Memorandum transmitting Information Note No. 69
subfiles.about: Transmits a requested financial statement on cotton advances to Japan.

subfiles.title: Financial Statement on Commodity Credit Corporation Cotton Advances to Japan
subfiles.about: Calculates advances for raw cotton shipped and delivered to Japan through March 1947.
subfiles.summary: The note distinguishes cotton shipped from cotton delivered and reconciles Commodity Credit Corporation and U.S. Commercial Company advances with textile-sale receipts. It reports net CCC advances of about $121.63 million for shipments and $112.63 million for deliveries.

subfiles.title: Moscow telegram on Red Star criticism of American loans to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports a Soviet newspaper review portraying American loans to Japan as anti-Communist policy.
subfiles.summary: Summarizes V. Avarin’s Red Star review of A. Roth’s book.

subfiles.title: Japanese Securities and Exchange Law
subfiles.about: Critiques Japan’s 1947 securities law and lists provisions needing implementing ordinances.
subfiles.summary: Wells argues that corporate disclosure and stockholder control should support deconcentration and prevent renewed zaibatsu power. He identifies omissions, duplication, drafting errors, and weak investigative authority in the new law, and recommends sending an expert to Japan. The attachment lists articles requiring ordinances.

subfiles.title: Telegram on reparations machinery and administrative questions
subfiles.about: Reports committee decisions on reparations machinery and requests personnel and budget information.
subfiles.summary: Reports approval of valuation procedures, discussion of pooled machine tools, and requests for personnel and 1948 budget updates.

subfiles.title: Swiss Legation memorandum forwarding a securities declaration
subfiles.about: Forwards another Swiss bank declaration concerning Japanese enterprise securities.
subfiles.summary: Requests forwarding of the enclosed Swiss Bank Corporation declaration through designated channels.

subfiles.title: Swiss Bank Corporation declaration of Oriental Development Company bonds
subfiles.about: Declares bonds held by a Liechtenstein citizen.
subfiles.summary: Lists $10,000 nominal value in six-percent Oriental Development Company bonds.

subfiles.title: Despatch forwarding Bank of Japan report on self-supporting economy and credit
subfiles.about: Forwards a Bank of Japan report on Japan’s economic recovery and foreign credit needs.
subfiles.summary: Notes the report’s timely credit discussion and questions some of its industrial statistics.

subfiles.title: Establishment of Self-Supporting Economy and Credit
subfiles.to: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Sets out a three-year plan for minimum economic stability and the foreign credit needed to achieve it.
subfiles.summary: The report projects production, transport, agriculture, consumption, employment, and trade through June 1950, while acknowledging persistent poverty and unemployment. It makes recovery dependent on imports of food, fuel, machinery, and textile materials, alongside expanded exports led by textiles. It estimates cumulative external deficits of roughly $1.05 billion and asks chiefly the United States for reconstruction and raw-material credits, relief financing, shipping assistance, and long-term repayment terms. The report continues after page 400.
